title: Pad See Ew
subtitle: Thai stir-fried wide rice noodles with dark soy and egg
excerpt: This is a wok dish where heat is everything. The smoky, slightly charred flavour that makes pad see ew distinctive comes from a very hot wok and the confidence to leave the noodles without stirring long enough for them to catch. Cook for two at most per batch.
sourceNotes: Pad see ew translates roughly as stir-fried with soy sauce, specifically the dark soy that gives the noodles their characteristic deep colour. The dish is a staple of Thai street food and is thought to derive from Chinese chow fun, brought to Thailand by Teochew immigrants in the nineteenth century.

content.text: Soak the noodles in cold water, not hot, so they are pliable but not cooked before they hit the wok. If you soak in boiling water they will overcook and disintegrate. The wok must be smoking hot before anything goes in.

items.prepNote: wide, soaked in cold water for 20 minutes then drained
stems cut into 2 cm pieces, leaves left whole

content.text: Combine the dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, oyster sauce, and palm sugar in a small bowl. Stir to dissolve the sugar and set aside.
Heat 1 tbsp of oil in the wok over the highest heat until smoking. Add the chicken and stir-fry for 2-3 minutes until just cooked through. Push to the side of the wok.
Add another 1 tbsp of oil and the garlic. Fry for 20 seconds, then crack in the eggs and scramble briefly until just set. Break into rough pieces.
Add the drained noodles and the sauce. Toss everything together once, then press the noodles flat against the wok surface and leave for 30-40 seconds without stirring so they colour slightly.
Add the pak choi stems and toss, cooking for 1 minute. Add the leaves and toss for a further 30 seconds until wilted. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Noodles clumped together in the wok.
items.cause: Not separated before cooking, or wok not hot enough.
items.fix: Separate the soaked noodles thoroughly with your hands before they go in, and make sure the wok is at full heat.

items.cause: Sauce added too early or wok not hot enough to evaporate moisture.
items.fix: Ensure there is no pooling liquid in the wok when you add the sauce, and use high heat throughout.
